scenes.text: In just a few days at the end of October, chip stocks lost roughly a trillion dollars in value. Intel fell almost thirty percent in a single day, its worst day in decades.

elements.credit: "New York Stock Exchange August 2017 02" by Arild Vågen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia
"Intel Headquarters in 2023" by Coolcaesar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia

elements.text: Intel stock plunges as chipmaker issues weak forecast

elements.label: Intel, in one day: worst in decades

scenes.text: But the strange part isn't the crash. It's where a lot of that money came from in the first place. Because when you follow it, some of it goes around in a circle.

elements.text: some of it goes around in a circle

scenes.text: By the end of this video, you'll understand the loop, why it made the AI boom look even bigger than it was, and the three signals that tell you whether this ends in a soft landing or a real bust.

scenes.chapter: The biggest building spree in history
scenes.text: Start with the spending. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta are on track to spend more than seven hundred billion dollars this year, mostly on data centers and the chips inside them.

elements.credit: "File:Building92microsoft.jpg" by Coolcaesar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia
"Googleplex HQ (cropped)" by The Pancake of Heaven!, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia
"2024-12-21, Amazon Spheres (Seattle), 170559" by Steven Pavlov, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia
"Meta Platforms Headquarters Menlo Park California" by LPS.1, CC0 1.0, via wikimedia

elements.text: mostly data centers, and the chips inside them

scenes.text: Alphabet alone guided to around two hundred billion. Meta, up to one hundred forty-five. Microsoft, about one hundred seventy. And next year, the total is expected to top one trillion dollars.
To put that in perspective: that's more than most countries produce in a year, spent on buildings full of computers, by four companies.

elements.text: More than most *countries* produce in a year

scenes.text: So what are they actually buying? A modern AI data center is a warehouse packed with racks of specialized chips called GPUs, wired together so thousands of them can work on one problem at once. Then you need cooling, because those chips run hot, and enormous amounts of electricity. The chips are by far the most expensive part, and that's what makes this story so interesting.

Why would anyone spend like this? Because to the people running these companies, the bigger risk is being too slow. Mark Zuckerberg reportedly put it this way: if Meta ends up misspending a couple of hundred billion dollars, that would be unfortunate, but falling behind in AI would be worse. Every company is thinking the same thing. And when everyone is afraid of being last, nobody wants to be the first to stop spending.

elements.credit: "Mark Zuckerberg - South by Southwest 2008" by Jason McELweenie, CC BY 2.0, via wikimedia

elements.text: Misspending a couple hundred billion would be unfortunate. Falling behind would be worse.

scenes.text: And this isn't just about chips. These data centers need staggering amounts of electricity. AI deals are now measured in gigawatts. One gigawatt is roughly enough power for several hundred thousand American homes. So a ten gigawatt deal means building computer warehouses that use as much electricity as a few million homes, and power plants and transmission lines to feed them.

elements.text: plus new power plants and transmission lines to feed them

scenes.text: And here's where it gets interesting. A big share of that money ends up at one company: the one that makes the chips.

elements.credit: "NVIDIA Headquarters" by Coolcaesar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia

scenes.text: Nvidia makes the chips most of the world's AI is built on, along with the software developers have used for years to program them. That's why buyers have had so few alternatives, and why Nvidia became one of the most valuable companies on Earth. Keep that in mind, because it explains the deals you're about to see.

elements.credit: "Jensen Huang - RTX 5070 Laptop - Nvidia Keynote - CES 2025 Las Vegas" by Pronoia, CC0 1.0, via wikimedia

elements.sub: the chips most AI is built on

elements.credit: "2788-2888 San Tomas Expwy" by Coolcaesar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia

scenes.text: Now meet the loop. Picture three players. A chip maker, like Nvidia or AMD. An AI lab, like OpenAI. And a cloud company, like Oracle or CoreWeave, that owns the data centers.

Step one: the chip maker invests money in the AI lab. Step two: the AI lab signs a giant contract to rent computing power from the cloud company. Step three: the cloud company uses that contract to raise money and buy chips from the chip maker.
And look what just happened. The chip maker's investment came back to it as revenue. The same dollars showed up as an investment on one side and as sales on the other.

This isn't a theory. In September twenty twenty-five, Nvidia announced it could invest up to one hundred billion dollars in OpenAI, while OpenAI planned to fill data centers with Nvidia chips. That plan was later reportedly scaled back to a thirty billion dollar stake. But the pattern stayed the same.

elements.credit: "Jensen huang stanford 2026-04-30 029" by Anderseidesvik, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia

elements.text: Nvidia plans to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI

scenes.text: Weeks later, AMD gave OpenAI the right to buy up to one hundred sixty million AMD shares, about ten percent of the company, as part of a deal for six gigawatts of AMD chips.

elements.credit: "AMD headquarter 20240318" by Lijiaxuan, CC0 1.0, via wikimedia
"File:AMD CEO Lisa Su 20150603.jpg" by Gene Wang, CC BY 2.0, via wikimedia

scenes.text: OpenAI also reportedly agreed to buy around three hundred billion dollars of computing from Oracle over about five years. And Oracle, to deliver it, has to buy enormous amounts of chips.

elements.credit: "Oracle Headquarters Redwood Shores" by Håkan Dahlström, CC BY 2.0, via wikimedia

scenes.text: Altogether, OpenAI's CEO has said the company is looking at about one point four trillion dollars of computing commitments over roughly eight years.

elements.credit: "Meeting with Masayoshi Son and Sam Altman (February 3, 2025)" by 首相官邸ホームページ, CC BY 4.0, via wikimedia

scenes.text: Now compare that with what OpenAI actually earns. At the end of twenty twenty-five, Altman said OpenAI was making about twenty billion dollars a year in revenue.
That's a seventy to one gap. Even spread over eight years, OpenAI would need its revenue to grow many times over, very fast, just to pay for what it has promised.

elements.text: Even over 8 years: still ~*$175B a year*
revenue would need to grow many times over, fast

scenes.text: Here's another way to see it. In late twenty twenty-five, OpenAI said ChatGPT had about eight hundred million weekly users. To cover one hundred seventy-five billion dollars a year, every single one of those users would need to pay roughly eighteen dollars a month. Most of them pay nothing today.

elements.label: from every user, to cover $175B a year

elements.text: …and most of them pay nothing today

scenes.text: OpenAI's own projections show it losing money for years, before turning profitable around the end of the decade. Even Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang said in twenty twenty-five that OpenAI doesn't have the money yet.

elements.credit: "Keir Starmer, Jensen Huang - on stage together at NVIDIA event, looking excited and positive 5256 2" by LAK7474, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia

scenes.text: So where does the money come from? Investors, and debt. And this is the part that matters most.

elements.credit: "Wall Street Sign (5899884048)" by Alex Proimos from Sydney, Australia, CC BY 2.0, via wikimedia

elements.text: So where does the money *come from*?

scenes.text: Many of the companies building data centers for AI labs, the so-called neoclouds like CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN, don't have the cash to build on their own. They borrow, often without investment-grade credit ratings.

elements.text: they borrow, often without investment-grade credit ratings

scenes.text: As interest rates rose this year, lenders started pulling back. The research firm Gartner even predicts that by twenty thirty, eighty percent of these neocloud companies will be absorbed or gone.

elements.label: of neoclouds absorbed or gone by 2030 (Gartner)

scenes.text: Think about what that does to the loop. If a cloud company can't borrow, it can't buy chips. If it can't buy chips, the chip maker's sales slow down. And suddenly the loop runs in reverse.

That's exactly the fear that hit the market last week. Even the giants are feeling it. Alphabet and Meta both reported negative free cash flow, meaning they spent more than their businesses brought in.

elements.text: Alphabet & Meta: spending more than their businesses brought in

scenes.text: There's one more hidden problem, and it's about time. An AI chip is not a building. It gets outdated fast, because every year a faster chip comes out. Yet the big tech companies spread the cost of their servers over about five to six years in their accounts. If those chips are really worth much less after three years, then today's profits look better than they really are.

Now add the debt. A data center builder might borrow money for many years to buy chips that could be obsolete in three. If the chips lose value before the loan is paid back, the lender is left holding a loan backed by old hardware. That's exactly why credit markets are the place to watch.

If this sounds familiar, it should. In the late nineteen nineties, telecom equipment makers lent money to their own customers so those customers could buy more equipment. It was called vendor financing.

elements.text: equipment makers lent money to their own customers

scenes.text: It made sales look incredible, right until the customers couldn't pay. When the dot-com bubble burst, Cisco, which had briefly been the most valuable company in the world, lost more than eighty percent of its value.

elements.sub: briefly the world's most valuable company

scenes.text: To be fair, today is not an exact copy. The biggest buyers, like Microsoft and Alphabet, are hugely profitable companies, and real people are paying for AI products every day. Some economists argue these circular deals simply spread risk around.
The real question isn't whether AI is useful. It clearly is. The question is whether the money flowing in a circle is being mistaken for money flowing in from customers.

So how does a bubble actually pop? Here's the simple math. Say investors expect a company to earn ten dollars per share next year, and they're excited, so they pay thirty times that. The stock is three hundred dollars. Now the forecast drops to eight dollars, and investors get nervous, so they'll only pay twenty times earnings. The stock falls to one hundred sixty. That's nearly half its value gone, even though the company is still making a lot of money.

That's what happened to Intel in October. One weak forecast, and the price investors were willing to pay collapsed in a single day. When both the expected profits and the excitement drop at the same time, prices fall much faster than the business itself.

elements.credit: "2200 Mission College Boulevard" by Coolcaesar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia

elements.text: when profit hopes and excitement drop together, prices fall fast

scenes.text: So there are really two ways this ends. The soft landing: AI revenue keeps growing fast, spending slows down gradually, and the loop turns into a real business. Some companies lose money, but the industry survives and grows into its spending.

The hard landing: customers don't pay enough, lenders pull back, cloud companies cancel chip orders, and the loop runs in reverse all at once. Sales that looked solid disappear, and stock prices fall far more than the actual businesses do. Which one we get depends on those three signals.

elements.text: which ending we get depends on three signals

scenes.text: So here are the three signals to watch. Signal one: Nvidia's earnings on November seventeenth. Watch not just sales, but how much of its growth depends on customers it has also invested in.

elements.credit: "Director Lê Nguyễn Thiên Nga and NVIDIA Founder and CEO Jensen Huang" by VQTCS, CC BY 4.0, via wikimedia

elements.text: How much growth comes from customers it *invested in*?

scenes.text: Signal two: borrowing. If neoclouds and data center builders struggle to raise debt, or pay much higher interest, the loop is slowing.

elements.credit: "File:Monochrome wall street sign (Unsplash).jpg" by Chris Li chrisli, CC0 1.0, via wikimedia

scenes.text: Signal three: real revenue. Watch whether AI companies' sales from actual customers grow faster than their spending. That's the only thing that turns this from a loop into a business.

And here's why this matters even if you never buy a single tech stock. If you own an index fund, a big slice of it, roughly a third, is technology companies. Your retirement account is already riding the loop.

elements.q: person looking at phone finance app

elements.label: of a typical index fund is tech (roughly a third)

elements.text: your retirement account is already riding the loop

scenes.text: That doesn't mean panic, and this isn't financial advice. It means know what you own, and understand that part of the AI boom is real growth, and part of it is the same money going around.

One practical step: open your retirement or investment account and look at the top holdings. If the same handful of tech names fills the top of the list in every fund you own, you're more concentrated in this one story than you might think. Knowing that is the first step, whatever you decide to do about it.

elements.text: same few tech names everywhere? you're more concentrated than you think

scenes.text: So, the AI money loop: chip makers fund AI labs, AI labs rent from cloud companies, cloud companies buy chips, and debt keeps the wheel spinning. As long as customers keep paying more, it holds. If they don't, the loop is where the cracks will show first.
Next time, we'll follow another hidden money machine. Subscribe so you don't miss it, and tell me in the comments: do you think this is a bubble, or the beginning of something real?
